questions.q: In this course, what does “adaptive CNV” mean?
options: A stretch of DNA present in more or fewer copies than normal
A DNA segment duplicated one extra time
A copy-number difference that is the result of adaptation rather than a defect
A chromosome segment cut out and put back in the reverse orientation
questions.why: adaptive CNV stresses that the copy-number difference is the result of adaptation; CNV is only a neutral description of a stretch of DNA being present in more or fewer copies than normal, a duplication is one extra copy, and an inversion is a reversal of orientation — none of them carries the idea of “adaptive”.

questions.q: What role does “adenine” play in DNA and RNA?
options: The base written G, which pairs with C
The base written A, one of the four main bases of DNA and RNA
One of the four bases of DNA and also the only one that gets methylated
The base that replaces T in RNA
questions.why: adenine is written A; guanine is the one written G, cytosine is the only base that gets methylated, and uracil is the base that replaces T in RNA. The base-pairing rule for DNA is A with T and G with C.

questions.q: “A different version of a gene; a person carries two, one from each parent” — which term is this?
options: Heterozygous
Homozygous
Copy number variation (CNV)
Allele
questions.why: An allele is a different version of the same gene; heterozygous and homozygous describe which two versions are carried (different or the same), while a CNV is an abnormal number of copies of a stretch of DNA.

questions.q: What does “aneuploidy” refer to?
options: Two sets of chromosomes, one from the father and one from the mother
A cell with an abnormal chromosome number, usually caused by failure of separation during meiosis
One chromosome present once instead of twice, written as 2n minus 1
Three copies of chromosome 21 instead of two
questions.why: Aneuploidy is a cell with an abnormal chromosome number, usually caused by failure of separation during meiosis; diploid is the normal state (23 pairs in humans), while monosomy and trisomy 21 are just two specific cases of it.

questions.q: In the context of DNA, what does “annealing” mean?
options: The process in which the double helix separates into two single strands of DNA, also called melting
The step in which polymerase adds new nucleotides along the template
The process in which two complementary single strands of DNA re-pair on cooling
The light-and-dark banded pattern formed after chromosomes are stained
questions.why: Annealing is the re-pairing of complementary single strands of DNA on cooling; separating the double helix is denaturation (melting), adding nucleotides is extension, and forming light-and-dark bands is G-banding.

questions.q: The two strands of DNA run in opposite directions, one 5′ to 3′ and the other 3′ to 5′; this property is called ______.
options: Antiparallel
Double helix
Base pairing
Denaturation
questions.why: The textbook calls “the two strands run in opposite directions” antiparallel; the double helix is the overall shape of the two strands wound around each other, base pairing is the rule for pairing bases, and denaturation is the separation of the two strands.

questions.q: What kind of DNA region does “AT-rich” refer to?
options: A DNA region with a high proportion of G and C in its base composition
The backbone in which sugar and phosphate alternate in the nucleotides
A DNA region containing only A and T, with no G or C at all
A DNA region with a high proportion of A (adenine) and T (thymine) in its base composition
questions.why: AT-rich means A and T are present in high proportion; GC-rich is the one with a high proportion of G and C, the structural framework of DNA is the sugar–phosphate backbone, and AT-rich does not mean there is no G or C at all.

questions.q: In 1943, ______ used DNase and protease to prove that the transforming factor was DNA.
options: Griffith
Avery, MacLeod and McCarty
Watson, Crick and Franklin
DNase
questions.why: The textbook credits the 1943 DNase/protease control experiment to Avery–MacLeod–McCarty; Griffith was the one who described the transformation phenomenon in 1928, and Watson, Crick and Franklin built the double-helix model.

questions.q: The base-pairing rule in DNA is ______ with T and G with C.
options: Thymine
Guanine
Adenine
Uracil
questions.why: The pairing rule given in the textbook is A with T and G with C; thymine is the one written T, guanine is the one written G, and uracil is the base that replaces T in RNA.

questions.q: What is the role of the “centromere” on a chromosome?
options: The narrow waist in the middle of the chromosome, where the spindle fibres grip the chromosome
The repeated sequences at the two ends of the chromosome, protecting the ends from degradation
The stretch of DNA wound around a histone octamer to form a nucleosome
The short arm and long arm on either side of the centromere
questions.why: The centromere is the narrow waist in the middle of the chromosome where the spindle fibres grip it; the repeated sequences at the ends are the telomere, DNA wound round histones is the nucleosome, and the p-arm and q-arm are the two arms.

questions.q: “DNA plus the proteins that package it; that is, the manual and its packaging” — which is it?
options: Chromosome
Nucleosome
Euchromatin
Chromatin
questions.why: Chromatin is DNA together with its packaging proteins (manual plus packaging); a chromosome is a complete bound copy of the manual, a nucleosome is the turn of DNA wrapped round histones, and euchromatin is the loose, active state of chromatin.

questions.q: What does the textbook compare a chromosome to?
options: A manual that has just been printed and not yet packaged at all
A bound copy of the manual that is the genome
A recipe that is being transcribed and left open
A machine that can copy DNA in bulk inside bacteria
questions.why: The textbook uses “a bound copy of the printed manual that is the genome” for a chromosome; chromatin is the manual plus its packaging, a gene is a recipe specifying one product, and a plasmid is a small circular DNA that can replicate on its own.

questions.q: Which is an example of “circular DNA”?
options: A nuclear chromosome, that is, one long straight piece of DNA plus protein
The human genome, a linear double strand of about three billion bases
Mitochondrial DNA, a circle of about 17 thousand bases
The product of PCR, a linear double-stranded DNA
questions.why: The example of circular DNA given in the textbook is precisely mitochondrial DNA (a circle of about 17 thousand bases); nuclear chromosomes and the human genome are linear, and a plasmid is also circular, but this item refers to mitochondrial DNA.

questions.q: “A stretch of DNA present in more or fewer copies than normal” — which term is this?
options: Copy number variation (CNV)
Aneuploidy
Allele
Inversion
questions.why: CNV describes how many copies of a stretch of DNA are present; an abnormal chromosome number is aneuploidy, a version of a gene is an allele, and a reversal of orientation is an inversion — the four operate at different levels.

questions.q: Of the four bases, only ______ is methylated, so the whole stage for the epigenetic machinery is built on it.
options: Adenine
Guanine
Thymine
Cytosine
questions.why: The textbook points out that of the four bases only cytosine is methylated, so the stage for DNA methylation and epigenetics is built on it; A, T and G are not.

questions.q: What does “deletion” mean at the DNA level?
options: A DNA segment duplicated one extra time
A stretch of DNA is lost
A chromosome segment cut out and put back in the reverse orientation
One chromosome present once instead of twice, written as 2n minus 1
questions.why: A deletion is a stretch of DNA being lost; one extra copy is a duplication, a reversal of orientation is an inversion, and one chromosome fewer is monosomy.

questions.q: What does “denaturation” (melting) mean for DNA?
options: The process in which two complementary single strands of DNA re-pair on cooling
The temperature at which half of the DNA double helix has come apart
The process in which the double helix separates into two single strands of DNA
DNA being chopped into fragments by an enzyme
questions.why: Denaturation is the double helix coming apart into two single strands; re-pairing on cooling is annealing, “the temperature at which half has come apart” is the melting temperature (Tm), and chopping DNA into fragments is the work of DNase.

questions.q: How does “deoxyribose” differ from the sugar in RNA?
options: It has one oxygen atom fewer than the sugar in RNA
It has one oxygen atom more than the sugar in RNA
It is a five-carbon sugar, whereas the sugar in RNA is a six-carbon sugar
It carries a phosphate group, whereas the sugar in RNA does not
questions.why: The textbook says the sugar of DNA is deoxyribose and the sugar of RNA is ribose, which differ by a single oxygen; the phosphate is the third component of a nucleotide (base + sugar + phosphate), and neither sugar carries a phosphate itself.

questions.q: What does “diploid” refer to?
options: One set of chromosomes, all from the mother
One chromosome present once instead of twice
One particular chromosome present three times instead of twice
Two sets of chromosomes, one from the father and one from the mother; human somatic cells have 23 pairs
questions.why: Diploid means two sets of chromosomes, one from each parent, 23 pairs in human somatic cells; monosomy is 2n minus 1 and trisomy is one particular chromosome having an extra copy — both are abnormalities of chromosome number.

questions.q: “Identifying an individual by differences in the length of repeated sequences” — which method is this?
options: G-banding
DNA fingerprint
Karyotype
PCR
questions.why: A DNA fingerprint identifies an individual by differences in the length of repeated sequences; G-banding is the light-and-dark banding after staining, a karyotype is the image of all the chromosomes, and PCR is a method for amplifying DNA — none of these is an identity fingerprint.

questions.q: “The enzyme that chops up DNA; it destroyed the transforming activity, and DNA was identified in this way” — what is this?
options: Protease
EcoRI
DNase
NotI
questions.why: When DNase chopped up the DNA the transforming activity disappeared, and this is exactly the evidence on which Avery–MacLeod–McCarty concluded that DNA is the genetic material; a protease cuts protein, whereas EcoRI and NotI are the restriction enzymes used in molecular cloning.

questions.q: What is the role of the “donor plasmid” in molecular cloning?
options: The plasmid that carries “the piece of DNA to be delivered”
The bacterium on the receiving end that accepts the recombinant DNA
The recombinant plasmid that carries the target DNA after delivery
The antibiotic resistance marker used to select bacteria that have taken up the plasmid
questions.why: The donor plasmid is the “sending end”, carrying the target DNA (the insert) to be delivered; the receiving end is the recipient plasmid, and what the two combine to form is a recombinant plasmid, while the resistance marker is Amp.

questions.q: How does the textbook describe the structure of the double helix?
options: Two DNA strands like two zips, with the bases pairing on the outside
One DNA strand wound into a screw, with the other sitting in the groove but not separated
Bases stacked in pairs into a cylinder, with no distinction between two strands
Two DNA strands wound around each other, with the bases pairing in the middle like the rungs of a ladder
questions.why: The textbook compares the double helix to a ladder: the two strands wind around each other and the bases pair in the middle like the rungs; the model built by Watson, Crick and Franklin is precisely this one.

questions.q: Which statement about Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is correct?
options: It is a structural abnormality of the chromosome, a segment reversed in orientation
It is an abnormality of chromosome number, one particular chromosome having three copies instead of two
It is a copy-number abnormality, an increase in the number of copies of a stretch of DNA
It is a change at the level of the gene, two different versions of the same gene
questions.why: Down syndrome is trisomy 21: chromosome 21 has three copies, so it belongs to aneuploidy; a reversal of orientation is an inversion, an increase in copy number is a CNV, and different versions of a gene are alleles.

questions.q: In the classification of tumour mutations, ______ is the mutation that actually drives the tumour and gives the cell a growth advantage, while a passenger merely hitchhikes.
options: Passenger
Copy number variation (CNV)
Driver
Silent mutation
questions.why: The textbook says a driver gives the cell a growth advantage — it is the wrong word in an important sentence; a passenger is merely carried along by chromosomal instability, and the two are told apart by integrating the CNV profile with mRNA expression.

questions.q: In the classification of CNVs, what does “duplication” mean?
options: A DNA segment duplicated one extra time
A stretch of DNA is lost
A chromosome segment cut out and put back in the reverse orientation
A stretch of DNA present in more or fewer copies than normal
questions.why: A duplication is one extra copy, while a deletion is a segment lost; “more or fewer copies of a stretch of DNA than normal” is the general term CNV, and an inversion is a reversal of orientation with no gain or loss of DNA.

questions.q: In the molecular cloning workflow, DNA is cut with ______ and NotI, and the nicks are then sealed by DNA ligase.
options: DNase
primer
plasmid
EcoRI
questions.why: The textbook names EcoRI and NotI as the two restriction endonucleases in the same molecular cloning workflow, after which DNA ligase seals the nicks; DNase is the enzyme that chops up DNA and is tied to the transformation experiment, not to a cloning step.

questions.q: “Loose, actively transcribed chromatin” — which one is that?
options: Heterochromatin
Euchromatin
Chromatin
Nucleosome
questions.why: Euchromatin is the loose, active chromatin; heterochromatin is the tightly packed, silent form that keeps transcription factors away from the promoter; chromatin is the whole thing, and a nucleosome is the turn of DNA wrapped round histones.

questions.q: The three steps of each PCR cycle are denaturation, primer annealing and ______, in which polymerase adds new nucleotides along the template.
options: Sanger sequencing
Substitution
Extension
Duplication
questions.why: Extension is the step in which polymerase adds new nucleotides along the template; the two earlier steps are heating to separate the strands and cooling to anneal, while words about sequencing and mutation do not belong to the PCR cycle.

questions.q: “A mutation in which the number of letters added or removed is not a multiple of three, so the reading frame shifts and the protein is usually truncated” — which class of mutation is this?
options: Frameshift
Missense mutation
Nonsense mutation
Substitution
questions.why: A frameshift is a shift of the reading frame caused by adding or removing a number that is not a multiple of three; a missense swaps one amino acid, a nonsense creates an early stop codon, and a substitution replaces a base.

questions.q: The resolution of G-banding is about 0.5–10 Mb; what practical consequence does this limitation have?
options: It can pin down a change of a single base
It can read out the complete sequence of the whole genome
It applies only to protein samples and cannot be used for chromosomes
It can reveal large structural changes but cannot see point mutations — point mutations need PCR/Sanger or NGS
questions.why: G-banding is the light-and-dark banding seen after the chromosomes are stained, with a resolution of only 0.5–10 Mb, so large structural changes are visible; point mutations can only be detected by PCR/Sanger sequencing or NGS.

questions.q: “A DNA region with a high proportion of G (guanine) and C (cytosine) in its base composition” — which term is this?
options: AT-rich
GC-rich
Melting temperature (Tm)
Base pairing
questions.why: GC-rich means a high proportion of G and C; AT-rich is the one with a high proportion of A and T, Tm is the temperature at which half the double helix has come apart, and base pairing is the pairing rule itself.

questions.q: What does the textbook compare a gene to?
options: A bound copy of the printed manual that is the genome
The narrow waist in the middle of a chromosome
A recipe: a stretch of DNA that specifies one product
A small circular DNA that can replicate on its own inside bacteria
questions.why: A gene is a recipe specifying one product (a stretch of DNA); a chromosome is a bound manual, the centromere is the narrow waist of a chromosome, and a plasmid is small circular DNA.

questions.q: What does “genome” refer to?
options: The complete set of DNA possessed by an organism or a cell
A different version of a gene
A stretch of DNA present in more or fewer copies than normal
DNA plus the proteins that package it
questions.why: The genome is the complete set of DNA of an organism or a cell; an allele is a version of a gene, a CNV is a difference in the number of copies of a stretch of DNA, and chromatin is DNA plus packaging proteins.

questions.q: When the number and structure of chromosomes keep going wrong so that the whole genome becomes unstable, that state is called ______.
options: Copy number variation (CNV)
adaptive CNV
Karyotype
genomic instability
questions.why: Genomic instability refers to the genome as a whole becoming unstable; CNV and adaptive CNV are only differences in the copy number of a stretch of DNA, and a karyotype is the tool for looking at chromosome abnormalities.

questions.q: “The 1928 bacterial experiment showed that material from dead Streptococcus pneumoniae could turn harmless live bacteria into disease-causing bacteria” — which scientist was this?
options: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty
Griffith
Watson, Crick and Franklin
DNase
questions.why: Griffith described the transformation phenomenon in 1928; Avery–MacLeod–McCarty used DNase and protease to show that the transforming factor was DNA, and Watson, Crick and Franklin built the double-helix model.

questions.q: What role does “guanine” play in DNA and RNA?
options: The base written A, which pairs with T
The only base that gets methylated
The base written G, which pairs with C
The base that replaces T in RNA
questions.why: Guanine is written G and pairs with cytosine; adenine is the one written A, cytosine is the only base that gets methylated, and uracil is the base that replaces T in RNA.

questions.q: “Chromatin that is tightly packed and silent, physically preventing transcription factors from reaching the promoter” — which is it?
options: Heterochromatin
Euchromatin
Chromatin
Nucleosome
questions.why: Heterochromatin is tightly packed so that transcription factors physically cannot get near the promoter and the gene is silenced; euchromatin is the loose, active form, chromatin is the whole thing, and a nucleosome is the turn of DNA wrapped round histones.

questions.q: “Carrying two different versions of the same gene, one from each parent” — which is it?
options: Homozygous
Allele
Diploid
Heterozygous
questions.why: Heterozygous means carrying two different versions of the same gene; homozygous means two identical versions, an allele is the version itself, and diploid is the state of having two sets of chromosomes.

questions.q: What does “homologous chromosome” refer to?
options: A sister chromatid copied from the same DNA, separating at meiosis II
One of a matched pair of chromosomes, one from each parent, separating at meiosis I
A different version of the same gene
The same chromosome cut out and put back in the reverse orientation
questions.why: A homologous chromosome is one of a matched pair of chromosomes, one contributed by each parent, and they separate at meiosis I; sister chromatids separate at meiosis II.

questions.q: What does “homozygous” refer to?
options: Carrying two different versions of the same gene, one from each parent
Two sets of chromosomes, one from the father and one from the mother
Carrying two identical versions of the same gene
One chromosome present once instead of twice
questions.why: Homozygous means two identical versions; heterozygous means two different versions, diploid is the state of having two sets of chromosomes, and monosomy is 2n minus 1.

questions.q: What is an “ideogram”?
options: A standardised diagram of a single chromosome with every band marked
An image of all the chromosomes of a cell, used to look for large structural abnormalities
The light-and-dark banded pattern formed after chromosomes are stained
The repeated sequences at the two ends of a chromosome
questions.why: An ideogram is the standardised diagram of a single chromosome with every band marked; the image of all the chromosomes of a cell is called a karyotype, the light-and-dark banded pattern is G-banding, and the repeated sequences at the ends are the telomere.

questions.q: In molecular cloning, the piece of target DNA that is delivered into the plasmid is called the ______.
options: plasmid
primer
vector
insert
questions.why: The insert is the piece of target DNA that is delivered into the plasmid; the plasmid is the vector itself, the primer is the PCR primer, and a vector is the general concept of a carrier that delivers nucleic acid into cells.

questions.q: If a chromosome segment is cut out and put back in the reverse orientation (an inversion), what feature does it have?
options: The total amount of DNA increases and the copy number rises
The total amount of DNA is unchanged, but gene expression may change
The total amount of DNA decreases and the segment disappears completely
The chromosome number changes from 46 to 45
questions.why: An inversion reverses the orientation and neither adds nor removes DNA, but pushing a gene away from its enhancer or bringing it to an inappropriate enhancer changes expression; a rise in copy number is a duplication, complete loss of a segment is a deletion, and one chromosome fewer is monosomy.

questions.q: “An image of all the chromosomes of a cell, used to look for large structural abnormalities” — which is it?
options: ideogram
G-banding
Karyotype
Karyotyping
questions.why: A karyotype is the image of all the chromosomes; karyotyping is the procedure that produces that image (Giemsa staining to give G-banding), an ideogram is the diagram of a single chromosome, and G-banding is the light-and-dark banding after staining.

questions.q: By what method is “karyotyping” done?
options: By Giemsa staining to produce G-banding, so that large structural changes can be read off directly
By differences in the length of repeated sequences to identify an individual
By winding DNA round a histone octamer to form a nucleosome
By chopping DNA up with an enzyme to destroy transforming activity
questions.why: The textbook says karyotyping uses Giemsa staining to produce G-banding so that large structural changes can be read off directly; differences in the length of repeated sequences are a DNA fingerprint, winding round histones is a nucleosome, and chopping up DNA is DNase.

questions.q: “The first separates matched chromosomes; the second separates sister chromatids” — what does this describe?
options: Homologous chromosome
Sister chromatid
Non-disjunction
Meiosis I and meiosis II
questions.why: This is precisely the division of labour between meiosis I and meiosis II: the first separates matched chromosomes, the second separates sister chromatids; homologous chromosomes and sister chromatids are what gets separated, while non-disjunction is separation going wrong.

questions.q: The temperature at which half of the DNA double helix has come apart is called the ______; the higher the GC content, the higher it is.
options: Denaturation
Melting temperature (Tm)
Annealing
Extension
questions.why: The textbook calls “the temperature at which half has come apart” the melting temperature (Tm) and points out that G–C has three hydrogen bonds while A–T has two, so the more GC there is the higher the Tm; denaturation is the process of coming apart, annealing is re-pairing, and extension is adding nucleotides.

questions.q: “A change of a single letter that swaps one amino acid for another” — which class of mutation is this?
options: Nonsense mutation
Frameshift
Missense mutation
Silent mutation
questions.why: A missense changes the amino acid; a nonsense creates an early stop codon that truncates the protein, a frameshift is a shift of the reading frame caused by adding or removing a number that is not a multiple of three, and a silent mutation does not change the amino acid sequence.

questions.q: What is the core procedure of “molecular cloning”?
options: Putting a chosen DNA fragment into small circular DNA and copying it in bulk
Delivering DNA directly into human cells as a treatment
Copying the entire genome in bacteria
Using PCR to linearise a fragment and splice it back into a chromosome
questions.why: Molecular cloning is putting a chosen fragment into small circular DNA (a plasmid) so that it is copied in bulk in bacteria; delivering nucleic acid into cells is the job of a vector or lipid nanoparticle, and PCR is responsible only for amplification, not for getting the fragment into the plasmid.

questions.q: What does “monosomy” refer to?
options: One particular chromosome has three copies instead of two
Two sets of chromosomes, one from the father and one from the mother
A chromosome segment cut out and put back in the reverse orientation
One chromosome is present once instead of twice, written as 2n minus 1
questions.why: Monosomy is 2n minus 1; three copies is trisomy, two sets of chromosomes is diploid, and a reversal of orientation is an inversion.

questions.q: “A misprint in a printed manual” — which term does the textbook use this metaphor to explain?
options: Frameshift
Mutation
Duplication
Karyotype
questions.why: The textbook describes a mutation as a misprint in a printed manual — in an unimportant passage it is only a misprint, but in an important one it can turn a normal cell into a cancer cell; the other terms describe a different change or an observational tool.

questions.q: What does “non-disjunction” mean?
options: A chromosome segment cut out and put back in the reverse orientation
A stretch of DNA present in more or fewer copies than normal
Chromosomes failing to separate normally during meiosis, producing an abnormal chromosome number
A different version of a gene
questions.why: Non-disjunction is chromosomes failing to separate normally, which directly produces an abnormal chromosome number (aneuploidy); a reversal of orientation is an inversion, a difference in copy number is a CNV, and a version of a gene is an allele.

questions.q: Why does a nonsense mutation truncate the protein?
options: It creates an early stop codon, so translation terminates prematurely
It swaps one amino acid for another, and the protein is still made as normal
It shifts the reading frame, so the downstream amino acid sequence is completely different
It increases the copy number of the gene, and the protein output rises accordingly
questions.why: The textbook says a nonsense mutation creates an early stop codon, so the protein is truncated; swapping an amino acid is a missense, a shift of the reading frame is a frameshift, and an increase in copy number is a CNV or a duplication.

questions.q: “The other restriction endonuclease used alongside EcoRI in molecular cloning” — which is it?
options: DNase
primer
plasmid
NotI
questions.why: The textbook names EcoRI and NotI as the two restriction endonucleases in the same molecular cloning workflow, after which DNA ligase seals the nicks; DNase is the enzyme that chops up DNA, the primer is the PCR primer, and the plasmid is the circular vector.

questions.q: About 147 bp of DNA wound round an octamer made of two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 — this structure is called a ______.
options: Chromatin
Nucleosome
Euchromatin
Heterochromatin
questions.why: The textbook describes the spool formed when DNA is wound round a ring of histones as the nucleosome (the crystal structure of Luger and colleagues was resolved at 2.8 Å); chromatin is the whole thing, and euchromatin and heterochromatin are its two active states.

questions.q: Which part of a chromosome does “p-arm” refer to?
options: The long arm
The narrow waist in the middle, where the spindle fibres grip
The short arm
The repeated sequences at the two ends
questions.why: The p-arm is the short arm and the q-arm is the long arm; the narrow waist in the middle is the centromere, and the repeated sequences at the ends are the telomere.

questions.q: The mutation that is carried along by chromosomal instability and does not itself confer a growth advantage is called a ______.
options: Passenger
Driver
Duplication
Nonsense mutation
questions.why: The textbook describes a passenger as a change that simply hitchhikes, in contrast to the driver that actually pushes the tumour forward; the two are told apart by integrating the CNV profile with mRNA expression.

questions.q: The three steps of the PCR cycle are denaturation, primer ______ and extension.
options: extension
denaturation
Substitution
annealing
questions.why: Each PCR cycle first heats to separate the two strands (denaturation), then cools to let the primer pair with the template (annealing), and finally the polymerase adds new nucleotides (extension), giving roughly 2ⁿ-fold exponential amplification.

questions.q: What is a “plasmid” in molecular cloning?
options: A linear chromosomal DNA plus protein
A small circular DNA that can replicate on its own and be expressed in bacteria
A restriction endonuclease used to cut DNA
An enzyme that chops up DNA and destroys transforming activity
questions.why: A plasmid is small circular DNA that can replicate on its own and be expressed in bacteria; it is what carries the insert in and makes it in bulk — it is neither a linear chromosome nor an enzyme.

questions.q: If the misprint in the manual changes only one base, this smallest unit of mutation is called a ______.
options: Frameshift
Structural variant
Point mutation
Copy number variation (CNV)
questions.why: A point mutation is the smallest unit of change; a frameshift is a shift of the reading frame caused by adding or removing a number that is not a multiple of three, a large rearrangement of chromosomal material is a structural variant, and a difference in the number of copies of a stretch of DNA is a CNV.

questions.q: What is a “primer” in PCR?
options: A short single-stranded DNA that pairs complementarily with the template and provides a 3′-OH starting point
The enzyme that cuts DNA into two strands
The enzyme that seals the new fragment
The high-temperature step that separates the two strands of DNA
questions.why: The primer is short single-stranded DNA that pairs complementarily with the template and provides the 3′-OH that lets the polymerase get going; cutting is done by restriction enzymes, sealing by ligase, and separation by heating (denaturation).

questions.q: What happens during the primer annealing step of PCR?
options: The primer is cut up at high temperature
The primer is joined to the end of a new DNA chain
The primer welds the two strands of DNA together
On cooling, the primer pairs with the complementary sequence on the template and lines up its 3′-OH end at the point from which synthesis will start
questions.why: Annealing is the primer pairing complementarily with the template on cooling and getting its 3′-OH starting point ready; extension is what adds the new nucleotides, while cutting and joining are the jobs of restriction enzymes and DNA ligase respectively.

questions.q: Why does “PCR need a pair of primers”?
options: One primer handles denaturation and the other annealing
The two primers anneal at the two ends of the target region, which is what defines and amplifies that stretch of DNA
One primer cuts the DNA and the other joins it
The two primers are used to deliver the product into bacteria
questions.why: PCR uses a pair of primers that anneal at the two ends of the target region, defining the region to be amplified and making the product increase exponentially; denaturation and annealing are steps driven by temperature, while cutting and joining are the work of restriction enzymes and ligase.

questions.q: In Avery's experiment the protease could not cut the transforming factor, whereas ______ could break it up, so the genetic material is DNA.
options: EcoRI
primer
DNase
plasmid
questions.why: The key control in the experiment is exactly that DNase destroys it while protease does not: once the DNA is chopped up the transforming activity disappears, while chopping up protein has no effect; EcoRI and NotI belong to the cutting step of molecular cloning.

questions.q: Once a chromosome is divided into a p-arm and a q-arm, how are G-banding band numbers read?
options: They are numbered by the arm they lie on and their distance from the centromere, so q21.1 is read as q-two-one-point-one, not q-twenty-one-point-one
They are numbered by base-pair count, from highest to lowest
They are numbered by whether the DNA is AT-rich or GC-rich
They are numbered by the age of the chromosome
questions.why: The textbook specifically warns that q21.1 is read q-two-one-point-one and not q-twenty-one-point-one; band numbers follow the arm and the distance from the centromere, not the base count or the GC content.

questions.q: What is the “recipient plasmid” in molecular cloning?
options: The plasmid that carries the target DNA to be delivered
The recombinant plasmid that carries the target DNA after delivery
The antibiotic resistance marker used to select bacteria that have taken up the plasmid
The plasmid on the receiving end that accepts the recombinant DNA
questions.why: The recipient plasmid is the receiving end; it is the donor plasmid that carries the DNA to be delivered, and what the two join to form is a recombinant plasmid, while the resistance marker is Amp.

questions.q: Once the donor plasmid and the recipient plasmid are joined, they form a ______ carrying the target DNA.
options: insert
recombinant plasmid
vector
primer
questions.why: A recombinant plasmid is the product that results when foreign DNA is joined into a circular vector; the insert is the piece of target DNA that is delivered in, a vector is the general concept of a carrier that delivers nucleic acid into cells, and the primer is the PCR primer.

questions.q: Why does the resolution of G-banding (about 0.5–10 Mb) matter for clinical interpretation?
options: It determines how deeply the chromosomes are stained
It determines how many times the nucleosome wraps the DNA
It determines which abnormalities are visible: large structural changes are visible, point mutations are not, and those need PCR/Sanger or NGS
It determines how many PCR cycles are needed for amplification
questions.why: Resolution is the upper limit of what can be detected: G-banding at about 0.5–10 Mb can only reveal large structural changes, and a change of a single base can only be judged by reading the sequence with Sanger or NGS.

questions.q: What is the role of “ribose” in nucleic acids?
options: The sugar of RNA, with one oxygen atom more than the sugar of DNA
The sugar of DNA, with one oxygen atom fewer than the sugar of RNA
The phosphate that links the nucleotides into the backbone
The base that determines the pairing
questions.why: Ribose is the sugar of RNA, while the sugar of DNA is deoxyribose, which differs by a single oxygen; the phosphate holds up the sugar–phosphate backbone, and it is the bases that determine pairing.

questions.q: The resolution of G-banding is only about 0.5–10 Mb and cannot see point mutations; to resolve a change of a single base you need ______.
options: G-banding
Karyotyping
ideogram
Sanger sequencing
questions.why: When it comes to the resolution of G-banding the textbook points out that point mutations can only be detected by PCR/Sanger sequencing or NGS; karyotyping and the ideogram are likewise chromosome-level observational tools.

questions.q: “The amino acid sequence is unchanged but the DNA sequence has changed” — which class of mutation is this?
options: Missense mutation
Silent mutation
Nonsense mutation
Frameshift
questions.why: A silent (synonymous) mutation does not change the amino acid sequence, which is what allows codon optimisation to swap synonymous codons; swapping an amino acid is a missense, early termination is a nonsense, and adding or removing a number that is not a multiple of three is a frameshift.

questions.q: “The two copies made from the same DNA, which separate at meiosis II” — what is this called?
options: Homologous chromosome
Allele
Sister chromatid
Chromosome
questions.why: Sister chromatids are the two copies produced from the same DNA; they come apart at meiosis II, and they are also why homologous recombination can find a template in S/G2 phase, whereas the first meiotic division separates the homologous chromosomes.

questions.q: What is a “sticky end”?
options: The single-stranded overhang left after a restriction enzyme cuts DNA
The repeated sequences at the two ends of a chromosome
The hydrogen bonds between the two strands of DNA
The contact surface between the nucleosome and DNA
questions.why: When a restriction endonuclease such as EcoRI or NotI cuts DNA it leaves a single-stranded overhang, a sticky end, which DNA ligase can later seal; the repeated sequences at the ends of a chromosome are the telomere, while hydrogen bonds and nucleosomes are matters of structure.

questions.q: Which statement about the two strands of DNA is correct?
options: Both strands start at the 5′ end and run in exactly the same direction
One strand is DNA and the other is RNA, with the RNA strand acting as the template
The two strands can replicate independently, each without needing the other
The two strands run in opposite directions (5′→3′ and 3′→5′), the complementary bases pair in the middle, and new DNA can only be synthesised in the 5′→3′ direction
questions.why: The textbook says the two strands of DNA run in opposite directions (antiparallel) with the bases pairing in the middle like the rungs of a ladder; since the polymerase can only synthesise along 5′→3′, the direction of the template strand fixes the direction of the new strand, so replication has to separate the two strands and use each as a template.

questions.q: “A large rearrangement of chromosomal material, such as a segment reversed in orientation” — which class of variation is this?
options: Point mutation
Structural variant
Silent mutation
Allele
questions.why: Large rearrangements of chromosomal material (such as inversion and translocation) are structural variants and can be read off on a karyotype and on G-banding; a change of a single base is a point mutation or a silent mutation, and different versions of a gene are alleles.

questions.q: What does “substitution” mean in a DNA sequence?
options: A stretch of DNA is lost
A DNA segment duplicated one extra time
One base is replaced by another base
A chromosome segment cut out and put back in the reverse orientation
questions.why: A substitution is a change in which one base replaces another; complete loss of a segment is a deletion, one extra copy is a duplication, and a reversal of orientation is an inversion.

questions.q: The TTAGGG repeat sequence at the end of a chromosome is called the ______; it shortens with every division and, once it reaches a threshold, the Hayflick limit and senescence appear.
options: Telomere
Centromere
p-arm
q-arm
questions.why: The telomere is the TTAGGG repeat sequence (3–20 kb); it shortens with each division and, once it accumulates to a threshold, you get the Hayflick limit and cellular senescence; cancer cells reactivate telomerase, with its internal RNA template, to lengthen the telomeres.

questions.q: What role does “thymine” play in DNA and in RNA?
options: Both DNA and RNA use T
RNA uses T and DNA uses U
It is the only base that gets methylated
DNA uses T to pair with A; in RNA, U replaces T
questions.why: The four bases of DNA are A, T, G and C, and RNA substitutes U for T; the base that gets methylated is cytosine, which has nothing to do with thymine.

questions.q: What is the difference between a transcription factor and a cis-acting element?
options: A transcription factor is a DNA sequence and a cis element is a protein
A transcription factor is a diffusible protein encoded by other genes; a cis element is a sequence on the same piece of DNA
Both can diffuse freely and act on any chromosome
Both are simply a stretch of sequence on DNA
questions.why: The textbook defines cis elements (promoter, enhancer, silencer) as sequences acting on the same piece of DNA, while trans factors are the transcription factors: proteins encoded by other genes that can diffuse and act elsewhere.

questions.q: What does “transforming principle” refer to?
options: A gene that makes bacteria antibiotic-resistant
The carrier that lets bacteria exchange genetic material
The substance that can turn harmless live bacteria into disease-causing bacteria, later shown to be DNA
A failure of separation that causes an abnormal chromosome number
questions.why: Griffith's experiment first showed that material from dead bacteria could transform live bacteria; Avery–MacLeod–McCarty then used DNase and protease to prove that this transforming principle was DNA.

questions.q: Translocation and inversion are both changes in chromosome structure; what is the difference between them?
options: An inversion cuts a segment out and puts it back on the same chromosome in the reverse orientation; a translocation joins a segment onto a different chromosome
An inversion joins a segment onto a different chromosome; a translocation reverses orientation within the same chromosome
Both increase the total amount of DNA
Both only change gene expression and leave chromosome structure completely unchanged
questions.why: An inversion reverses the orientation with no gain or loss of DNA, whereas a translocation attaches a segment to a different chromosome; both are large-scale structural changes that can be read off on a karyotype and on G-banding.

questions.q: What does “trisomy” refer to?
options: One chromosome is present once instead of twice
Two sets of chromosomes, one from the father and one from the mother
A stretch of DNA present in more or fewer copies than normal
One particular chromosome has three copies instead of two
questions.why: Trisomy means one particular chromosome has an extra copy; monosomy means one copy fewer, diploid is the normal two sets, and a CNV is a difference in the number of copies of a stretch of DNA.

questions.q: What is the upstream mechanism that produces Down syndrome (trisomy 21)?
options: A restriction enzyme cutting the wrong position on chromosome 21 and causing a translocation of the segment
Chromosomes failing to separate normally during meiosis (non-disjunction), so that chromosome 21 ends up in three copies
Telomerase shortening the telomeres at the ends of chromosome 21
Methylation of cytosine switching off all the genes on chromosome 21
questions.why: The textbook lists trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) as an abnormal chromosome number caused by non-disjunction; translocation, telomere shortening and methylation never give a chromosome an extra copy.

questions.q: What is the chromosomal feature of “Turner syndrome (45,X)”?
options: Three copies of chromosome 21 instead of two
A chromosome segment cut out and put back in the reverse orientation
Only one X chromosome, written as 45,X, that is 2n minus 1
A stretch of DNA present in more or fewer copies than normal
questions.why: The textbook sets 45,X alongside trisomy 21 as outcomes of non-disjunction: Turner syndrome is one sex chromosome missing (2n minus 1), whereas Down syndrome has an extra chromosome 21.

questions.q: “Bisulfite treatment converts unmethylated cytosine into ______, which is read as T after PCR” — which base is it?
options: uracil
adenine
guanine
thymine
questions.why: When describing bisulfite sequencing the textbook says that unmethylated cytosine is converted into uracil, which is read as T after PCR; methylated C is retained, so uracil here is precisely the signal of “unmethylated”.

questions.q: What is the shared role of a “vector” in molecular cloning and in gene therapy?
options: The restriction endonuclease that cuts DNA into fragments
The sequencing method that reads out the DNA sequence
The antibiotic resistance marker used to select bacteria that have taken up the plasmid
The carrier that delivers DNA into cells: a plasmid in molecular cloning, and more broadly adenoviruses and lipid nanoparticles also qualify
questions.why: The textbook says a vector is the carrier that delivers nucleic acid into cells — in molecular cloning a plasmid that replicates on its own and is expressed in bacteria, and more broadly adenoviruses and lipid nanoparticles count too; cutting uses restriction enzymes, sequencing uses Sanger, and selection uses Amp.

questions.q: On what two lines of evidence was the double-helix model built?
options: Griffith's bacterial experiment and Avery's enzyme experiment
Franklin's X-ray diffraction image (the X-shaped pattern), together with the rules known at the time: the amount of A equals the amount of T, and the amount of G equals the amount of C
The chemical structure of the bases and the structure of DNA polymerase
The G-banding pattern of chromosomes and the karyotype image
questions.why: The textbook says the model rested on two lines of evidence — Franklin's X-ray diffraction image and the base-ratio rules known at the time — and that Watson and Crick combined the two to propose the double helix; Griffith and Avery answered the different question of whether it was DNA at all.
